utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, would you --

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you state your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Sakir Tac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Turkish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is your first language Turkish?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But are you able to understand the Albanian language?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I understand it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So today we'll be speaking using the Albanian language, but if there is any moment when you don't understand something that you hear from one of the interpreters, would you please tell us so --

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- that we can make sure your testimony is clear.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I agree. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are you also able to understand the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I understand it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, where was your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I was born in Mamusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is Mamusa in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Mamusha, yes, it's in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And your date of birth, Mr. Tac, when was that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: 5th of March, 1954.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Farmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you were a younger man, did you perform your military service in what was then the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What did you do in the army?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I was in the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where do you live today?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: In the village of Mamusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you live in Mamusa in 1999, Mr. Tac?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Today, are most of the residents of Mamusa of Turkish ethnicity, like you?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Ninety per cent Turkish and 10 per cent Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in 1999, were most of the residents of Mamusa also Turkish, with a minority of Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did any Serbs live in Mamusa in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: There have never been Serbs in Mamusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: 1999, approximately what was the normal population of Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: In the village of Mamusha alone?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Tac, I'd like to show you a map, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask the usher for some assistance now. We have a map which will need a number, if Madam Registrar could also assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if copies of this map could be distributed to the Judges, to the accused, to the amici, and one to the Registry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- and if a copy could be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I could ask that map could be projected on our screens so that everyone can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, I'd like you to take a look at that map, and hopefully you'll be able to --

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- identify some areas on it. Where -- in what municipality, first of all, is the village of Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: In Prizren municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Could you take up the pointer that's on the desk in front of you and point on the map that's on that projector and point out where Prizren --

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Here. Prizren is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And let's go a little bit more slowly, please. And where is the village of Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Tac, if you could, could you pick up a pen - and hopefully there's a pen on the table in front of you - and draw a circle where your village is.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you could, Mr. Tac, could you write your initials, ST, next to that circle, please.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tac, apart from Mamusa, were there any other towns or villages -- are there any other towns or villages in that area of Kosovo where the population is mostly of Turkish ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Apart from Mamusha, there were Turks in Prizren, in Prishtina, and in other towns a few, but really only in Mamusha there were Turks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. That exhibit could be removed from the ELMO now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, I'd like to ask you, please, to turn your mind to the events of March 1999, if you will. In March of 1999, was there any KLA presence --

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- in Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: There wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At the same time, around March of 1999, did the Serb police patrol in Mamusa from time to time?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They often came to watch the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Mr. Tac, do you recall when NATO forces began bombing in parts of Kosovo on the 24th of March, 1999? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was there ever any NATO bombing in Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the NATO bombing in Kosovo make you afraid?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, they didn't. We were on their side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you be a little bit more specific as to what -- when you say they didn't make you afraid --

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, we weren't afraid. We were all there in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you and your family remain in Mamusa throughout the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. We were all in Mamusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What happened, Mr. Tac, in Mamusa on the evening of the 25th of March, 1999? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, in Mamusha, at about 10.00 at night, a whole group of refugees came, about 1.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you know, Mr. Tac, where did these refugees come from?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They came from the surrounding villages. They all came from the villages round about to Mamusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the refugees who came to Mamusa that night?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you speak to any of them?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: The whole village was absolutely crammed full of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did any of these refugees stay in your house that night?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did they tell you -- did any of them tell you why they came to Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. They said because it was quiet. To save their lives, that was why they came to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So why would they come to Mamusa, why would these refugees come to Mamusa to save their lives? What was special about Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Mamusha was very quiet at this time. There had been no conflicts. They had come to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And approximately how many people of Albanian ethnicity sought shelter in Mamusa beginning on the 25th of March?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, they came about 10.00 at night. We didn't see them, so we couldn't tell how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: By the next day, could you give an estimate as to how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has said a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: He did say a thousand on that night, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. No. On that day, we didn't see, but when we came out after two days later, there were about 30.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, let's move forward to the events of 27 March 1999. Were you in Mamusa on that day?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, in Mamusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What happened on the 27th of March, 1999 in Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: On the 27th of March, 1999, at about 10.00 or 11.00, the army came, with tanks, and entered Mamusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at this time I'd like to show you an exhibit, Mr. Tac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if the usher could assist me again to show Exhibit 17 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, I'd like to ask you to take a look at the photograph that has been placed on the projector next to you. A minute ago, you said the army came in tanks, and I'm wondering if you could look at the photographs --

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- if you could look at the photographs on those pages on the projector and see if you can identify a photograph containing a tank as you know it, the kind of tank that came on the 27th of March. Can you take a look on the projector next --

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: There are none of them here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, can you put another page on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There. They had -- they had long barrels.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what number? Which photo, which number of photo are you pointing to, Mr. Tac?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If those photographs could be removed now, please. And if we could have Exhibit 18 placed on the ELMO as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, I'd like to ask you to take a look at the photographs that are on the exhibit that's to your left and see if you can identify the -- a photograph or photographs containing the uniform resembling the uniforms worn by the soldiers that came to Mamusa on the 27th of March, if it's there in that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Number 5. They were camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Are there any other photos that also resemble the uniforms that you saw?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: The soldiers in green like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And which number are you pointing to now?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. That can be removed now. Mr. Tac, when the Serb army first arrived in Mamusa on the 27th of March, where were the residents and the refugees that day?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: In among the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was the atmosphere like?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They came to the middle of the village -- into the middle of the village with tanks, and the refugees were among the houses, and they told us all to come out into the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at some point did the residents and the refugees leave their houses and come to the centre?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We all went out with all the refugees and all the villagers of Mamusha into the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, is there a road that runs through the centre of Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, there is. There is a road. It is a long one, and all the road was full of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did anyone give any instructions to the people gathered in the centre at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: The soldiers came in among them. I don't know who they were, but they came in, in around the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were any instructions given to the people at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Everybody was ordered to go out into the middle of the village, the residents and the refugees alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what happened when all the people had gathered in the middle of the village?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. We went out of the houses and left the houses empty, and we went out into the middle of the village and they said to us, "You of Mamusha go on one side, and you refugees on another side."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you say on one side or the other side, are you referring to the road that runs through the centre of Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. No. The population of Mamusha at one side and then the Albanian refugees separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. What language did the soldiers speak?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you able to understand what they said?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, we understood. They said, "Separate yourselves. Refugees on one side."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did the people -- did the people gathered there follow the soldiers' instructions and divide into two groups, separate themselves?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We separated into two groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, why did the people follow the army's instructions on that day?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We -- we were afraid. What else could we do?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when the people were divided into two groups that day, what did the soldiers or their commander, if there was one, say to the people?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They said, "You people of Mamusha bring out your carts, buses, trucks, everything you've got, and fill them with refugees and take them away from here."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did you feel at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: He told me to get trucks and fill them with refugees, and all our friends came out on the street with these vehicles and parked them there and started to fill them up with people, all the buses and trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did any of the displaced persons, the refugees who were in Mamusa on that day, have their own vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some, but those carts were left in the yards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the soldiers -- or what, if anything, did the soldiers tell the refugees to do with their vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We filled those carts and cars that had come out, and then they asked, "How did all these people get to Mamusha?"

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was the response?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We told them that they had come with tractors and horses and carts and anything that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then what, if anything, did the soldiers say to do with those tractors and trailers and carts belonging to the refugees?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: All our vehicles were filled up, and they said, "All right. Don't you use your carts, but let them go out with all their own carts and let them all go out in the streets with what they have."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at that time, did any of the refugees bring their own vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. Those who had their carts went back and fetched them, whatever they had, and they got on board, and then they set out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's go a little bit more slowly, Mr. Tac. Were the soldiers in Mamusa carrying weapons that day?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. They were all armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you feel that the people had any choice as to whether to obey the soldiers or not that day?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: The people had no choice. We had to obey their orders. There was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. nothing we could do about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did any of the displaced Albanians that you saw, any of the refugees that you saw in Mamusa that day, have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: You mean the Albanians? No, the Albanians didn't have any weapons. If they did, they would have killed us. They were simply refugees: children, women, elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were any of the refugees that you saw, the Albanians, wearing a uniform that day in Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you notice any planes bombing in the area that day?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you see a battle going on or hear the sounds of a battle taking place on that day?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. In Mamusha village, there was never any fighting, not only that day, but never; never in the past did we have any fighting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At some point was a convoy made of the vehicles owned by the refugees in Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a convoy of refugees. We, the inhabitants of Mamusha, were sitting aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you own a truck, Mr. Tac?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you use your truck on that day or did you remain in Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: That day, I did not use my truck. Other friends of mine did. I, no; I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you watch the convoy of vehicles when it left Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. We all saw them leave for Prizren or I don't know where they were taking them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On that day, did the Albanian residents of Mamusa remain in Mamusa or did they also join the convoy?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They were in Mamusha together. We were all together there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So just so that the record is clear, the Albanians who lived in Mamusa stayed there on that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. They stayed together with us, the Albanians of Mamusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, after the convoy and the refugees left, did the commander of the soldiers say anything to the people who remained behind in Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a commander. I don't know who he was. He told us that all women, elderly, and children should go back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what happened after all the elderly and women and children went back to their homes?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We remained there. Then they gathered us together in the middle of the village, all of us villagers of Mamusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was said to the villagers of Mamusa at that time by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: One of them got on a ladder and then he said to us, "Look here, you villagers of Mamusha. If you do something against us, we are going to burn your homes and to kill you." And we said, "No, we are not going to do anything to you."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so that the record is clear, the translation that I heard says that one of them got on a ladder. Would it be more accurate to say that one of them got on a staircase?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was a small staircase, and he got on top of it. In front of a shop, it was. And he told us, "If you fire at us, if you do something against us, we are going to kill you, to burn your homes." We said, "No, we aren't going to do anything against you," and we never did, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in fact, at any time, Mr. Tac, during the day of the 27th of March, or that evening, did anyone from Mamusa shoot at the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. We went back to our homes, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned before that some of your friends from Mamusa were driving vehicles in the convoy that left that day towards Prizren. Approximately what time did your --

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. They left. First there were the buses, trucks from Mamusha that left to Prizren, then the refugees got on their own cars and, as I said, we were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, I understand that, so I'd like you just to listen to my question. My question is: Approximately what time did your friends who drove vehicles in that convoy return to Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know. We didn't see them that night. We saw them on the next day but not that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. On the following day, did you have an opportunity to speak to any of your friends who had driven a vehicle in that convoy?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did they tell you where they had taken the refugees?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. They told us that they had taken the refugees to the border with Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's talk now, Mr. Tac, about the evening of 27 March, 1999. On that evening, where were you?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I was at home. All of us were at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what happened in Mamusa that evening?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: That night - it was about 6.00 in the afternoon - we saw that the houses of the village started to go in flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was it dark?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, it was dark. About 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how were you able to see what was happening?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We were in our own homes and then we saw flames coming out of some houses. We were inside. It was from a distance. We could see the smoke and the flames. We were -- we went to our cellars to hide there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: About how many houses were burned in Mamusa that night?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: About 30, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did anyone in those houses die as a result of the fires that night?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: That night, we didn't know what was happening, I mean in terms of people who got killed or injured. On the next day, we found out that seven people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the persons who perished that night in Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Three Turks, four Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At some point during that evening, the 27th of March, did a tank come near the village of Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. A tank was coming in the direction of Mamusha. When it came in the village, we went to a brook nearby. No. I'm sorry. The tank had an accident and rolled over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who did the tank belong to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: It belonged to the army, the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say that the tank rolled over, where did this tank roll over?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: It rolled over about 200, 300 metres above the village it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After this tank rolled over, were more homes set on fire in Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We didn't know what was happening, but we found out that this burning stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Did you actually see the tank where it was lying when it rolled over?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I didn't see the tank that night, but on the next day when they came to pull it over with a crane, we saw the army troops passing by in the middle of the village to go to the place where the tank had the accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you able to see who started the fires in Mamusa on the evening of 27 March?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I didn't see who set the fire, but people there know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The following day, on the 28th of March, did you discuss the fires with any of the people who fled the burning homes?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They left, and then the army came and they set fire to the houses, and they drove us away from our homes. It was the Serb Yugoslav army that did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, did anyone tell you that it was the Serb army who set fire to those homes?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. The Serb army has burned the homes, and they drove us away from our homes, and they killed seven people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, my question is: Who told you that? Do you recall who told you that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Our villagers who left their homes, they told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on the 28th of March, was there a funeral in Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a funeral. We buried the people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's move forward now to the events of the 2nd of April, 1999. Mr. Tac, on that day, were you at home in Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Mamusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At about noon on April 2nd, what happened in Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of April - it was in the afternoon at about 12.00 or 1.00 - the police came to the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Approximately how many police came to Mamusa that day?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Five or six, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did the police tell the people in the centre of the village to do?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They -- they told us to give us [as interpreted] our trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure --

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: To give them our trucks. They needed our trucks. This is what they told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the police want the villagers to bring their trucks somewhere?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They wanted us to bring out our trucks to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, did you hear the police give this order or did someone tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I was at home, and someone told the villagers who went to the middle of the village. He said, "All of you bring out your trucks to the road."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how were you informed about this order?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Some of the trucks were about to leave, and a neighbour of mine came up to me and said, "You, too, should come out with your truck."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so what did you do?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I took my truck and I drove to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you reached the road, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: When we reached the road, we parked beside the road and we were waiting for them to tell us what they wanted us to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you were parked in a line along that road, did you see the policemen there on the road?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. The police were coming around the cars and trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were the police armed that day?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, did you come to learn the identity of any of the police at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question really was: Did you learn the identity of any of the individual policemen who were in Mamusa on that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I didn't know any one of them, but some of my friends said that this policeman is called Sipka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I could, I'd like to ask the usher's assistance one more time, and if we could show Exhibit 18, have that placed on the projector, please, once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, I'd like to ask you to please look at the photographs that have been placed to your left, and if you can, if you could point out a photograph that shows the uniforms or uniform worn by the policemen on that day.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: This blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Which number -- which photograph number were you pointing to? Is that 4?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: This one here. The blue, number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That exhibit can be removed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, while you were parked in your truck on the road, did any of the other drivers from Mamusa arrive late or even without their truck?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: A friend came and said, "My truck has broken down."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did the man known as Sipka, known to you as Sipka, say to this friend whose truck had broken down?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: He said, "Come out with your truck in five minutes, otherwise I'll burn your house."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What language did Sipka speak?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you close enough to hear him?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. I was just there by my vehicle and he was forced to bring his vehicle and come.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Eventually, Mr. Tac, about how many trucks were lined up along that road?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: There were 12 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when all the trucks were lined up, what, if anything, did the policeman known as Sipka do?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: He walked along the trucks and told us to start them up, get ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We started the trucks up and got into the vehicles, and he was in front and we were behind him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you and the other drivers follow Mr. Sipka in your trucks?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. We all went after him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why? Why did you follow him?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Well, he told us to come out in our trucks and set off after him. We were forced to set off after him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when the trucks left the village of Mamusa on that day, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: To Medred, Xerxe, and then to Pirana.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is there a road junction in Pirane, an intersection?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: There's a crossroads to Rahovec and to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did Mr. Sipka stop anywhere?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: He stopped at Pirana and told us -- and indicated to us with his hand: Go up there towards Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you and the other drivers continue driving towards Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We went on towards Rahovec, and when we arrived in Xerxe, the police stopped us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did the police who stopped you in Zrze tell you to do?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: In Xerxe, they pointed us towards Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And eventually did you pass through Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We were directed to Rahovec, and the police in Rahovec stopped us again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did the police who stopped you in Rahovec tell you to do?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They told us to go to Malisheva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Mr. Tac, eventually did you arrive in the centre of Malisheva?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. We went to Malisheva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did you see when you arrived in the centre of Malisheva?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: There were a lot of refugees in Malisheva, and Serbian police and soldiers surrounding the refugees there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say "a lot," could you describe what you mean by "a lot"?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: There were -- I can't give you a number, but there was an unimaginable number of refugees there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Mr. Tac, what was the ethnicity of these refugees in Malisevo that day?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you arrived in Malisevo that day, did you see any planes dropping bombs?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. We didn't see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you hear the sounds of shooting or of a battle taking place?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear anything like that. I only saw refugees, policemen, and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you parked in the centre of Malisevo, what, if anything, did the police do?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: The police told us to get down and to open down the gates of the trucks. So we opened up the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Then they told the refugees, "Go on. Get into the trucks."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did the refugees there in Malisevo get into the trucks?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They did, and the trucks were filled up and we closed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, how did you know that the people there in Malisevo were refugees?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They were refugees. Malisheva was absolutely full. All the area -- the entire area of Malisheva had gathered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question is: How did you know that these people were -- that these people were refugees who had gathered in Malisevo? Did you speak to any of them?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We spoke to them and said, "Here you go. Go on, get into our trucks."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll move on. After the trucks from Mamusa were filled with people, what, if anything, did the police tell you to do?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. I was in the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. After the refugees, as you called them, got into the trucks, what, if anything, did the police tell you to do? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They said, "You set off for Prizren." They said, "Go on. When they're full up, off you go."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, how did you and the other drivers know where to go?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They said -- beforehand they said, "Fill up the trucks and then go to Albania." They told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And did you then begin to drive towards the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We set off from Malisheva to Rahovec, Xerxe, Pirana, Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Along the route, were you stopped along the way?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, they stopped us at Ostrozub. The Serbian army stopped us at Ostrozub, about ten kilometres from Malisheva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did these soldiers do when they stopped you?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They stopped us and asked for money from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What language did these men speak?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you give them any money?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They forced us to give them some. I had about 500 marks, and I was forced to give them to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After you gave these men some money, did you continue to drive towards the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They held us up about 20 minutes and then we set off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you continue to drive towards the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. We continued on toward the Albanian border.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Along the way, did you see any planes dropping any bombs?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. Rain was falling. We didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Along the way, did you see any battles taking place or hear the sounds of a battle?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, were you able to drive as far as the Albanian border that evening?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We couldn't get to the border that night. We went as far as Zhur.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, is Zhur a village close to the border of Albania?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: It's about six kilometres away. I don't know exactly, but six or seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Why did you stop --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, while they were driving to the Albanian border, was there any Serb police or army with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They -- they weren't with us along the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If there were no Serb forces driving with you along the road, why did you continue to drive towards the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: There wasn't, but they told us to take these people straight to Albania. So we were forced to take them. There was nothing else we could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, why did you stop in the village of Zhur?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: When we came to Zhur, the road was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say the road was closed, do you mean that the road was -- was full or jammed, or what do you mean by "closed"?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: It was full of trucks and buses. You couldn't -- you couldn't continue. It was just absolutely full. And we came up against this truck and had to stop ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So the road between Zhur and the boarder was full. So you couldn't go any further; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We couldn't go any further, uh-huh, so they had to walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you stopped in Zhur, did you say anything to the Albanians in your truck?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. We told them, "Okay, friends, we have reached Zhur. We can't go any further. We'll have to wait for two days. Can you get off and go on by foot towards Albania?"

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how did the people in your truck respond to that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They said, "Where are we?" "We're in Zhur." "Is the border far?" And I said, "It's six or seven kilometres, no further than that."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then did the people in your truck leave the truck?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: "All right," they said, "Thank you for taking us this far." And they got off and got out of the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was there any discussion then?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. "Thank you for bringing us this far. You brought us as if by plane." And we said goodbye and we said, "Safe journey," and we went one direction, they went in another. And we said, "God willing, you'll be all right," and we went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say, "We went back," what did you and the other drivers do?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We were 12 trucks and we returned to Prizren again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you stopped along the road before you got to Prizren?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. The police stopped us in between Zhur and Prizren, along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When the police stopped you at that time, did they ask you anything?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They asked us, "Where are you going?"

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how did you respond?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We told them that we are those people whom you ordered to take the people to the border, so we are going back home now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what response, if any, did the police make to you?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: The police told us, "Go to Prizren and let everybody know that you are there."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where specifically in Prizren did you have to go?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We went -- at the entrance to Prizren, all of us went and reported that we were back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say "we reported," who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Then at that time, when you reported to the police in Prizren, what, if anything, did the police in Prizren tell you and the other drivers to do?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: After we reported there, they said, "You should go back to Malisheva and get another wave of refugees."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you then drive back to Malisevo to pick up more people?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, we did not go. We said to them, "We don't have fuel, so we can't go." They held us up there for about two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And after about two hours, where did you --

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: After two hours, they let us go, and we set out for our own homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you and the other drivers return to Mamusa at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, we returned to Mamusha, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the assistance of Mr. Usher again. If we can place the first map that was shown to Mr. Tac a few minutes ago, if we could place that map back on the ELMO, Exhibit 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, you see I've put the same map on the projector next to you, and if you would, I'd like to ask you to help us out, please, to explain the route that you took from Malisevo to the village of Zur that evening. Could you pick up the green marker that's on the desk in front of you and could you draw a line to show the route that you took from Malisevo, going towards the border with Albania, to the village of Zur on the 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender Exhibit 51 for admission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, could he give us an estimate of that distance?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Approximately how many kilometres would it be to drive from Malisevo to Zur, Mr. Tac, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I can't give you an accurate figure, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: About how long did the drive take you on the evening of 2nd April?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We didn't have -- we were not in a state of mind to see, to watch the time. Maybe it took us about two hours, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At this time, if there's no objection, I would tender Exhibit 51. May I have the Court's indulgence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's start from the end, the end of what Mr. Tac has just been saying. Malisevo was full of refugees, you said; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, were those refugees able to be put up somewhere there in Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They were outside. When I saw them, they were gathered in the middle of Malisheva. There was no place they could go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means it was logical that somebody should take them away from that place, where they had nowhere to go, nowhere to be put up, to be evacuated somewhere, to be taken away to safety somewhere; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They wanted to take refuge somewhere from that place. They didn't have anywhere to go to be put up there, did they?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They didn't tell us that we are going somewhere. The police told us to go and pick them up and take them to Albania. The refugees didn't say anything to us themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did the refugees say to you?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Nothing. They just got on our trucks, and we drove them in the direction of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that they didn't have anywhere to take refuge and to be put up in Malisevo. That's what you said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. I said what I did. I mean, I spoke about the people I took to the place. I don't know what happened to the others. The others were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You helped them leave Malisevo, take them away. And you said that they weren't able to take shelter anywhere or be put up anywhere in Malisevo because there were so many of them. So do you consider that you helped those people?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Of course I helped those that I took in my truck, but I don't know what happened to the others that were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the ones that you took with you. You helped them. You helped them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's agreed to that. He's agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Second, you said that you weren't escorted by either the army or the police en route while you were taking away the refugees you helped.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. We were not escorted, I said, up to Pirana. The police escorted us up to Pirana. After Pirana, we were alone. Then in Malisheva, the police appeared again and then we left for the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you say the police appeared again? Where was that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Xerxe, Rahovec, again in Malisheva. The police and the army were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you left Malisevo and took the refugees that you helped. You took them off. And the police stayed in Malisevo, according to your own explanation. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when you arrived after, as you yourself said, two hours journey to Zur, was it raining all the time?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, it was raining.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you stop off anywhere along the road for somebody to get out for any of their needs, requirements, to get some water or things like that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We stopped only in Ostrozub where the army stopped us. After that, after Ostrozub, we didn't stop anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Didn't the refugees ask you to stop for them to be able to see to some of their needs?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. No. Who saw to their needs then? We had just to move in the direction of the border, and we stopped nowhere along the route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were the refugees hurrying to get there as soon as possible or was it only you who was in a hurry because of your truck?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They were sleeping while we were driving. They didn't know where we were driving them. They had no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Didn't they hear what you heard yourself because they were right next to you? So if they told you to drive them off towards Zur or Albania, how come the Albanians didn't hear that? How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell him to repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Malisevo, you were told to take them off towards the border, to drive them towards the border; is that right? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: In Malisheva, the police and the army told us, "Drive straight to the border. Take these people there." And this is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the people you were driving? Did they hear that? Did they hear the same thing you heard, what they told you, or were they far away from you? Were you told that in secret or were the people present too?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I was in my cabin. I was driving. They were behind. I don't know if they heard this or not. They told us driver to do that -- drivers to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But a moment ago you said that the others didn't know about it, didn't know where they were going. Now you say you don't know if they heard or not where they were being taken. So did they hear or did they not hear? Which of the two is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't -- he can't answer -- wait a moment. Wait a moment. Wait a moment. He can't answer for them. Now, it appears not very much turns on this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Tac, you said earlier that when you took the refugees to Zur, they said to you -- they asked you, "Is the border far?" And you said, "It's no more than six or seven kilometres." And the people said to you, "Thank you for taking us this far." And you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They thanked us for having brought them so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doesn't it mean that they knew already that they were heading to the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if they knew or not. We just told them that, "This is Zhur, and from here, the border is about six, seven kilometres," and I don't know what happened to them after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's where I was going to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said you stopped off after Zur because the road was closed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was closed because there were many other vehicles that were on the road which were standing there in front of you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, because of the other vehicles, buses, trucks. We had to stop there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you stopped at the end of this column?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, we stopped at the end of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you wait for the column to move forward?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We didn't know when the column would start to move forward. We didn't have time to wait there for two days. If we -- if -- we told the refugees, "If you don't want to walk, we can drive you," but they said, "Okay, we will walk."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you didn't have time to wait for the column to start moving forward.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Maybe we had time, but this is what we told them. "Can you walk?" And they said, "Yes," and they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you or did you not have time? You said you didn't have time to wait, so that you told your passengers, the people on the trucks, that they should go on, on foot.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We had time, but they said we would have to wait a long time here, so they set off on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who decided that they should set off on foot? Did you decide that or did they decide that? Did you decide to tell them to get off and go and continue their journey on foot or did they think it would be better for them to continue on foot? Which of the two is it?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We ourselves, all we drivers gathered together, and we said, "Okay. Can you get off and continue on foot?" And they said, "Okay," and they continued on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then they thanked you for bringing them thus far; is that right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago while you were testifying, "We told the refugees that they couldn't go any further and that they should get off the trucks and continue their journey on foot." That's what you told them, according to your own testimony. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We told them, "You would have to wait a long time here, and you could set off on foot," and they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So that means they set off on foot because they accepted your proposal to do so; is that it?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, on foot. It's true; they set off on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We've been over this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. If we've come to that observation, I don't mind. I can go on. But let me go back to the beginning now. I wanted to clear up this matter first, what we've just heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, were you ever in hospital up until now?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long did you spend in hospital?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Twelve days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you leave hospital?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: This was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about these recent weeks. Were you in a hospital recently, in the past few weeks?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, I haven't been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So since 1994, you haven't been to hospital; is that it?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, I haven't been since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. According to information that I have here, throughout the war, in the village of Mamusa, it was completely quiet. Is that right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Mamusha, during those days, between 24th of March and 2nd April, it was quiet, and then we stayed in the village there. It was not quiet then, but then later on it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were two checkpoints set up by the police on both sides of the village, and life was quiet in the village; is that true? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said that, apart from the times which he's described in his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no checkpoint at Mamusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not in Mamusa. I said near Mamusa, not in Mamusa. There weren't any in Mamusa.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I didn't go anywhere after 2nd of April. I didn't see any checkpoints. I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the locals, during the war, kept an unexploded rocket, air rocket? Did you see that air rocket? They kept it in Mamusa. Missile, sorry. Missile.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see this. No bombs fell on Mamusha, and I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You live in the northern part of Mamusa and you have your own private shop in the house in which you live; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, we don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from farming, are you a truck driver?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I drive my own truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the village, up until the war, was inhabited 90 per cent by Turks and 10 per cent by Albanians and that that's how it remained after the war as well, that the population structure is 90 per cent Turks, 10 per cent Albanians. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The same. That's right. The same after the war too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that nothing has changed compared to before the war, nothing has changed in the village of Mamusa since before the war?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, nothing has changed. It's the same. Nothing has changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to my information and the figures, up until the war, the whole village of Mamusa lived in a normal way, as loyal citizens to Serbia, and I also have information that you would go out to all the elections that took place from 1990 to 1997. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: For myself, I didn't go to the polls. I don't know what the rest did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the locals from Mamusa went to the polls regularly, regardless of the fact that you say that you yourself didn't? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He says he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In the village, there is a primary school, and the director of that primary school was Abdul Tac, a Turk; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, Abdul Tac. That's right, a Turk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you cousins or related in any way?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, we're not. We're fellow villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The director of the clinic in the village is also a Turk; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, a Turk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the director of the post office too, also a Turk; right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, he's a Turk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Director of the chicken farm, Refki Mazik [phoen], also a Turk; right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: He died. Refki died a long time ago. And the farm doesn't work; it doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's 11.00. We're going to adjourn now. Mr. Milosevic, no doubt you will explain the relevance of those last few questions after the adjournment. Mr. Tac, we're going to adjourn, as I said, for half an hour. During the adjournment, don't speak to anybody about your evidence and don't let anybody speak to you about it, including members of the Prosecution team. Let me add this before we adjourn: We will sit this afternoon until a convenient time for a break, about a quarter to 4.00 or so, and thereafter we'll hear the submissions on the written statements before adjourning at half past 4.00. Half past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You asked what the relevancy of my question was. The thing is that in normal life with normal interrelations and an indubitable display and exercise of human and political rights that was enjoyed by Turks in Kosovo and Metohija. Do you remember that, just before the aggression, that Prizren was twice visited by representatives of the Turkish embassy, who talked to Turkish political parties both from Prizren and Mamusa and that at that time mutual satisfaction was expressed between -- with the relations between the authorities and the members of the Turkish minority? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Tell me the question again. I don't know. I'm not a politician. I'm a villager. I'm a peasant. I don't know about these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know about a visit to Prizren by representatives of the Turkish embassy just before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember certain members of the KLA from Mala Krusa, Pirana, Samodreza, and Studencane who hid for a while at your place?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know about this. I had no connection with the KLA. I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you asserting that not a single time before the war were there any members of the KLA who found shelter at your house, from the villages I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. There weren't. Not at my place, and I haven't seen any in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember the time when just after those members of the KLA were there, the police made a search of a part of your village? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: You mean the KLA was in the village and the police searched? No. I never saw anything like that. The police often came, and I am a peasant, and I was in the fields and at home, and I never saw things of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who were those Albanians whom you mentioned as being killed, those four Albanians? Do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They are from the village of Mamusha. Three Albanians and four Turks. The villages of Mamusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that on the 11th of April, and that was a Sunday, the 11th of April, when you were in Mamusa, according to your own words, do you remember that that day the members of the Turkish ethnic community from the village of Mamusa and from Prizren organised in Prizren a rally to convict -- condemn the aggression of NATO, and it was attended by 15.000 citizens?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, Your Honour. Just so that the record is clear and that the witness is not confused, he was never asked about the events of the 11th of April during --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. So it's something else. Mr. Tac, you're being asked about the 11th of April, and it's said that there was a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- a meeting there or a rally. Can you help us with that? What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no rally in Mamusha, but the police forced us to hold a rally. They forced us. They sent us to Prizren. And if we wouldn't go, they would burn our houses. We couldn't do anything else. What else could we do?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, 15.000 people were at that rally. Are you claiming that all of them were forced to go there? And they were mainly Turks.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: There were not 15.000 in Mamusha. Those from -- in Mamusha, there were 5.000, 6.000. We were forced and sent by force to the rally, and otherwise we would have had our houses burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said from Mamusa and Prizren. And the rally was held in Prizren, and almost the entire Mamusa attended. Are you claiming that that was not so?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We were all there. We were all there but by force. By force we were sent. We had either to go or they would burn our houses. What else could we do? We had to go. I didn't want to go, but they made me go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you participated in that rally against NATO on the 11th of April because you were forced.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. Of course we were forced. There's nothing else I could do. I had no other way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many people were there at that rally, in your opinion, because you attended?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know. There were a lot, but I saw -- I saw --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing can be done by force.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Nothing can be done by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Adem Koc addressed the rally, among others? He was president of the local commune in your village and also a representative of the Turkish Democratic Party, a Member of Parliament in the Municipal Assembly of Prizren?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I didn't know that he was a representative of Mamusha. Perhaps he spoke. I was at a distance. I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you had never seen him. You're saying you'd never seen him?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. He lives in Mamusha, but I had no idea he was the chairman of the local village. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that, at the same rally, Sadik Tanjoll also addressed the rally? He was president of the Turkish Democratic Party of Yugoslavia, an attorney-at-law.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know who spoke. We were a long way away. We were at the edge. What they said, what they did, I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know who Zenel Abedil Kures is? Have you ever heard of him? He's also a Turk.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I know that he's a Turk, but I don't know what he said. I'm not interested in this. I'm not a politician. I'm a peasant. I mind my own business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You must know that he was -- that Mustafa Bakir was headmaster of the primary school Zenel Abedil Kures.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that he addressed the rally?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Perhaps I spoke. All sorts of people spoke. But I'm not interested in who spoke, and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that Sokol Kushe [phoen], an Albanian, made a speech there? He's a director of a cultural institution in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know who he is. I don't know. I don't know him at all. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Franjo Prenglusha, also an Albanian, also a deputy of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know any of these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think this topic is exhausted. The witness says he doesn't know who spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I won't ask him any more about the Turks who addressed the rally, but I do wish to ask him, in this connection, if he remembers that the transport from Mamusa to Prizren was organised by private hauliers from the village of Mamusa, namely, Mamusha Tours and Birlik. Does he remember that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: What was organised? To go where?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Transport to Prizren, to the rally. The hauliers were your own from Mamusa. The Birlik enterprise and Mamusha Tours. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We were with our own vehicles. I don't know. I was with my own truck. All the people, everybody was with their own vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you went in your own vehicle to the rally, where you went under duress?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember, sometime in mid-May, or more precisely, on the 13th of May, when the president and members of the Executive Board of Kosovo and Metohija came to Mamusa with a trailer truck of humanitarian aid containing food and other essential products, both for Mamusa and other villages with the Turkish ethnic minority, sometime in mid-May?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was a big event. Your entire government visited.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I've never seen that. I never left my home. I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know anything at all about the 30th of May; that is, after that, the KLA kidnapped the president of the local commune and a deputy to the Assembly of Prizren, this Adem Koc person I already mentioned, and Morina Mahmet, who were held for questioning for several days in a basement in the village of Celina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you know those people and you know they were kidnapped? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know. I've never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that one of the most wealthy people had all his trucks confiscated?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that. I don't know. What time? At what time was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before the aggression. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Before the aggression, I was in Turkey. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you come back from Turkey to Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I came back in January 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that happened precisely at that time. How come you don't know about it?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
