utterances.text: When I returned home, I never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware that even before the aggression, and even now, the KLA took money to finance its terrorist organisation from the citizens of the village of Mamusa, that it racketeered the people of Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know. They never took any money away from me. I haven't heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware that during the war the work organisation Liria, from Prizren, opened a shop in Mamusa to supply the locals with essential products? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We had our shops in Mamusa, and we still have the same shops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that during the war, Mamusa was supplied in the way I described. Do you remember that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: That I don't know. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember the wounding of a Turkish woman, Suzana Taskra, during the bombing? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: You mean in Mamusha village?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. In Prizren.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, that I don't know. I know nothing about any other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: She worked at the TV station, broadcasting in Turkish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He says he doesn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that in the Turkish language, Radio Pristina, Radio Prizren, Radio Mitrovica, Radio Gnjilane broadcast in the Turkish language? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We didn't have electricity, and we heard nothing during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You never listened to the radio and you never watched TV?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. I said we didn't have power.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If you didn't watch television or listen to the radio, do you remember that there were newspapers in Turkish, such as Tan, Cergetush [phoen], Bai Cevrin, Esin, and Sofra?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't read papers. I am a farmer. Those who read know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the Sofra newspaper, published in Mamusa in the Turkish language?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I knew that it came out, that paper was published, but I don't read. I said, I don't read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know that they were published, but you didn't read them; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't read newspapers, but I know that such a newspaper was, and still is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that the Turkish Democratic Party had its own offices in the centre of Prizren? Were you a member of any party?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I have never been a member of any party, so I know nothing about this party. I am a farmer. I mind my own business. I work. I don't care about parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And have you heard of the death of an entire Turkish family on the 7th of April, the Gash family; mother, father, and four daughters? They were Turks. They were not killed in Mamusa. They were killed during the bombardment somewhere in town. Have you heard of that family?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Where were they killed? I don't know that. I never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you perhaps heard that the Turkish journalist Sarife Turgut, a correspondent of the ATV television, a Turkish television, described the rescuing of a 2-year-old girl who was saved by Dr. Andric from Pristina? Do you remember that event? There was a special programme on Turkish television about that.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Nothing. Nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything about, after the arrival of NATO troops in Kosovo, the 7-year-old daughter of Orana Kasma, from Prizren, was kidnapped and a very large ransom was demanded?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know nothing about it? And do you know about the rape and killing of a married Turkish woman, Ajsa Altiparmak, again after the arrival of NATO troops, and that was done by KLA terrorists?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. I have never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've put these matters very fully. He says he doesn't know. There seems little point going on putting incidents about which he is not aware. So perhaps you'd move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you are probably right. As you see, the witness doesn't know anything about what had been going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got any more questions about his evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in the village of Mamusa itself -- please listen carefully. In the village of Mamusa itself, on the critical day which you discussed a moment ago, that a large group of armed KLA terrorists from the villages of Studencane, Mala Krusa, and Pirane opened fire on the patrol of the MUP of Serbia, harming even innocent passersby?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Where was that event you are talking about? I don't know. What place was that? I don't know. In Mamusha, we have never had such an event. We have never had a clash between the KLA and the police. I don't know what you are talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about what you have just mentioned, that several people were killed in Mamusa.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: The Serb army killed them. Nobody else did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that you don't know who had killed them, that you didn't see that, you just heard of it. So how do you know that Serbs killed them?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: You said -- you said these people were killed, but they were not killed in the roads, in the streets somewhere. They were killed in their very homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how were they killed?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: That night we were at home. On the next morning, they were found. Their bodies were found in their own homes. And we buried them on the 28th of March, on the Bajram day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did they die? How were they killed? Were they killed by a bomb, a bullet, a stone?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: By the bullet, not by the bombs. We didn't have bombs in Mamusha. By arm -- by gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are now saying that they were killed from firearms, and a moment ago you said that you had never heard any shooting in Mamusa, whatsoever. So how could they have been killed by firearms?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, just a moment. The time that he was talking about was before the -- before there was trouble in the village. What he said was there was no bombing on that day or fighting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me note that he first said that he had never heard any shooting whatsoever, and a moment ago he said that people were killed during a shoot-out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not my --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So both cannot be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not my recollection that he said he heard no firing on the night of the 27th of March, which is the night we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the critical day that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'm saying -- I claim that they were hidden in his house. Part of the KLA members were in his house, in hiding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let the witness deal with that. Mr. Tac, what he said is that members of the KLA were in your house. Is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there isn't any truth in that. If they were in my home, we would have all been killed. But we didn't have any KLA members in my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does he know that the Albanian terrorists burnt the Serb village of Novak, only four kilometres away from Mamusa, with 80 Serb houses? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't in Novak. Perhaps they were burnt, but I was not there. I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you go to Prizren?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see that a tombstone of Nari Rexhalebia [phoen] was demolished in Prizren? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: It wasn't destroyed. It's still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't damaged at all, not even damaged?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't destroyed. It's still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the Turkish fountains in the yard of the mosque in the Tahban settlement destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it. I wasn't in that area. I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Osman Efendi mosque in Novo Brdo was completely destroyed? Did you hear about that from anyone, for example?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Where is that? Isn't that a church? I have never been to Novo Brdo. I don't know where it is. I don't know where Novo Brdo is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you hear about the fact that, in Prizren, people were sacked? Now, I'm talking about now, after KFOR, that Turks were sacked from their jobs, and their name was Xhala Jash [phoen], Fikrija Nush [phoen], Mehi Bekazaz [phoen], Nurik Malta [phoen], Jaku Plav, Mustafa -- from the Mustafa Bakija primary school, as well as Jakusha Mamushe [phoen]. Do you know about all of them or any one of them who were fired from their jobs?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I don't deal with schools. I am a farmer. I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did your children go to school?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, in Mamusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which language was tuition? Was it in Albanian when they went to school?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: It was in Turkish. They didn't go on to studies. They went on to be farmers and went to school in Turkish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you had a school in the Turkish language. Do you know that there were in fact six schools in the town and in the village of Mamusha itself with tuition in Turkish? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: There were not six schools. There was only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: There is one school in Mamusha. There were no -- aren't six schools. It's not a town. It's a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said one in Mamusa and the rest were in Prizren. Do you know about four secondary schools in your municipality where pupils were taught in the Turkish language as well?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know, but my children didn't go. I don't know what goes on there. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know about doctors, Turkish doctors, Bulent Krilje, Dr. Isak, Muxhada Kovic [phoen], Resmije Shata, Dr. Valkan [phoen] and others, all of them Turks, all of them working and offering treatment to patients? Have you heard of them?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know these doctors. Perhaps they work in this way, perhaps they don't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about Judges, Sas Kofiki [phoen], and Skender Musbeg, those two Judges? Have you heard of them? They are also Turks.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. This is the first time I've ever been in a court. This is the first time I've ever testified. And I don't know these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about Abdul Tac? Was he the headmaster of the primary school in the village of Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been through this once already. I don't think we're getting anywhere. Now, let's move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Prizren two Turkish drama theatre companies were functioning, with performances all over Yugoslavia and in Turkey and in Germany too? Have you heard of those?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I -- I've never had any chance to go and see these theatres. I've never been there. I don't know whether they've been in Yugoslavia and in other countries. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you at least know about the village of Mamusa and the cultural and arts society Askferki that functioned there in your own village? Do you know about that? In Turkish, the Turkish Cultural and Arts Society. Have you heard of that one?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is there and it's still there today, and it's working again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any Turks who were members of the government of Kosovo and Metohija, members of the Executive Council, as it was called, of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: One of them, a man, Zenel Abedil Kures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He doesn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking him whether he's heard of Zenel Abedil Kures. He was a minister there and a Turk. He must have heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of him, Witness? No?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard about a lady, also a Turkish lady, Bude Hasaru?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is -- this pointless. This is a pointless cross-examination. You have really put your case on this topic very fully. Now, have you got any other matters you want to ask him about his evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all this has to do with his evidence, but he doesn't seem to know anything about anything that went on except the fact that he helped a group of Albanian refugees to get out of Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about Adem Koc, Sadik Tanjoll, Zenel Abedil, Muhammed Ustaibar [phoen], Ilija Micamil [phoen], Hasan Merdan? Do you know of any of those individuals? They're all Turks.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Adem Koc is from the village of Mamusha, but for the others, I've never heard of them. And what they say, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about Mahmet Morina and Haim Shala, those two names? Also two Turkish gentlemen kidnapped by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know about this. I imagine that they're somewhere in Serbian prisons. I don't know who kidnapped them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why do you think they would be in prison in Serbia? They were loyal citizens of Serbia and didn't come into conflict with the authorities at all.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: This is what they say in their families, that sometime they'll emerge alive from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A Turk appeared who was in prison in Serbia. Is that what you're saying? What was the name of this one Turk?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now getting a very long way from the indictment in this case. Mr. Milosevic, speaking for myself, unless you have some relevant questions to do with this witness's evidence, I shall suggest to my colleagues that we bring your cross-examination to a close.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that refugees, the refugees that you speak about in Mamusa, asked the authorities to assist them to leave the area in which they were in jeopardy? And you took part in that assistance.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know about this. We opened our doors to them at night, and they had come to save their lives and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you give your first statement with respect to your testimony, and who did you give that statement to?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I didn't know these people. It was one year ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who did you give the statement to?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They came to the village of Mamusha and they asked who took the people to Malisheva, and we spoke up and we gave our testimony. There were eight of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who came?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't know them. I don't know who they were. They were from UNMIK or somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they Turks or Albanians or did they belong to some other ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They were from UNMIK. They weren't Turks. They spoke English or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You wrote in your statement that they asked you whether you knew anything about the bodies of dead people who were transported in trucks. Who asked you that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know about the bodies. I transported people who were alive. I don't know about this other case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but who asked you about that, about those dead bodies? Who asked you about that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: These UNMIK people, or I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did they in fact ask you?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: "How did you go to Malisheva to carry all these people?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but with respect to the dead bodies, they asked you something about that.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about dead bodies. I don't know anything about this business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said, in response to the question whether you knew anything about dead bodies: "I said that I was not mixed up in anything like that and have no information about that." That's why I'm asking you: Who asked you that particular question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said the people from UNMIK. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for giving me the floor. I don't have many questions, but Mr. Slobodan Milosevic insisted upon one point, and that is to be found in the last sentence of the statement which Mr. Sakir gave on the 10th of June, 2001. And I should like -- I haven't got much, but I would like to have that sentence presented to you, Your Honours, and the statement, because I have several questions in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we have copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sakir, first of all, let me start off by asking you the following, something you talked about at the beginning of your testimony. You said that your village was quiet, that there were never any conflicts there - you used the word "conflict," I believe - and that these people came to your village to take refuge.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear from them or anybody else that in other places, in other villages, there were conflicts?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: If they didn't have any conflicts, they wouldn't have run away from their homes and come over to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So conflicts between the KLA and the army; is that it?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: That I don't know, but there were problems there. There were conflicts. They came to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did members of the KLA ever come to your village?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. I've never seen them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you said previously, in paragraph 3 of your statement that Mr. Sakir gave on the 10th of June, 2001, in that third paragraph, it states the following: The KLA did not have a stronghold here, but they did come from time to time. There was no stronghold here, but they did visit from time to time. That is what you say in your statement, that they came from time to time, in your statement of June 2001. Is that what you said or not?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... say that. No, I didn't say that they have come to our village, no. I haven't seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain, then, how come this sentence exists in your statement, the statement you made at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: That I don't know. I never said that KLA came to Mamusha village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. On the 27th, the event took place which you have described to us here.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, the army or the police - it doesn't matter - searched houses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We left our homes, we went outside, they searched, then we went back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And all the houses were searched. Nothing was stolen from your house, but it had been ransacked; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, it was ransacked, but they hadn't taken anything away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean -- you know that they said that they were looking for weapons, just weapons, and as they found no weapons, did they take anything else from the house or not?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know what they searched for. We never had any weapons, nor do we have today. But I know that they searched. That is all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that there were casualties and that you buried them the next day. Do you know the names of any of those people from your village who were buried on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know the names of all of them. I know the names of the Turks, but I don't know the other four. I don't know the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also spoke today about the fact that you know, but you didn't see it, that a Serb tank was overturned there. You heard about that but didn't see it. That's what you told us today.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I didn't see it with my own eyes at that moment. On the next day, on the 28th of March, at about 10.00, when the forces came to pull that over with a crane, we saw it. We saw them passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why the tank overturned? Was it hit perhaps? Did anything hit it or was it overturned for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Nothing was there. The street was very narrow, but nothing happened. It was because of the very narrow street, and the tank was too large for that street.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the day that you drove the truck for two hours and were not accompanied by the police, you arrived at Zur, you came across the column of vehicles that had been stopped, that was stationary?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I am not clear about this question. What do you want me to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just repeating what you yourself said, that you arrived at the column that was standing still and that you couldn't go forward, and this was after two hours of driving. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you then suggested that they continue their journey on foot, and that's what they in fact did; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There was no army or police anywhere en route from that point where they started out on foot; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They were the Ostrozub army troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that. That's why I didn't ask you. But you drove for two hours, arrived at the point you stopped at, from which you couldn't continue further, and that was the spot where you made your suggestion to them. What I'm asking you now is: At that particular spot, there were no police or army, were there?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I didn't see any police or army troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You went back to your village and stayed there. Did you ever hear that in Kosovo a bomb had dropped of any kind, which was not from -- which did not come from a weapon owned by the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm coming to an end, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I don't know where that place was. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but what I'm asking you is: Was there any NATO bombing or not?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: In my village, no. I don't know about other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about other places, whether it happened in other places?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Maybe there has been in other places, but I don't know who did the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that you had no electricity in the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We didn't have electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why, why you didn't have any electricity?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: That I don't know. How could I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that many powerplants had been hit and they were the supplies and source of your electricity? Everybody knew that, that they had been hit.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: The powerplant in Kosova was not destroyed. I don't know what you are saying here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, I'd like to ask you to help us clarify a few points that were raised during the cross-examination. You were asked a few questions about the statement that you gave in the year 2001, particularly regarding a paragraph early in your statement, the third paragraph, and I'm going to read to you what the statement says and then I'm going to ask you a question about it. The third paragraph says the following: "Until March 1999, there had not been too much trouble in the village. Serbs would come and search, looking for people, maybe KLA. There was no stronghold here, but they did visit from time to time." Now, Mr. Tac, my question for you concerns the word "they" that you used -- that is used in your statement in the last sentence that I read to you. When you said, "but they did visit from time to time," by "they," were you referring --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Who was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: I have never seen any KLA members. I meant the police and the army, who often came to the village. But I never saw any KLA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That sentence reads precisely as follows: "The KLA did not have a stronghold here, but they came occasionally." So the KLA is mentioned in this sentence as not having --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not what the English says. No doubt we can have it looked out in due course. But the point has been made. Anything else, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The accused asked you whether you knew whether the refugees staying in Mamusa had asked the authorities to assist them, to use his expression. The refugees in Mamusa, or at least some of them, came to Mamusa in their own vehicles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could those refugees who arrived in Mamusa with their own vehicles have used their vehicles to go to the border if they had chosen to?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: First of all, they told them to go with your [sic] cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but that wasn't really what I was asking you about. My question was very simple: Could the refugees have simply gotten into their vehicles and gone to the border had they chosen to?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, because they were sent in our cars. But then the commander who -- it came to the mind of the commander, and he said, "How did these people get here in the first place?" And we told him they had come with tractors and cars and horses and carts. And they said to us, "Okay. Now they can go and get their own cars."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before members of the Serb army arrived in Mamusa on the 27th of March, could the refugees staying in your home and in other homes in the village, could they have left the village and gone to the border if they had wanted to?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. They were inside the village. I don't know what was in their minds. They came to us, to our houses, and there they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's move forward to the 2nd of April, when the police came to Mamusa and you left Mamusa that day, in a line with other trucks, escorted by the police in the beginning. Did you know what you were going to do that day?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, we didn't flee from -- we didn't leave -- flee the village. They forced us to go out onto the road to go to Malisheva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you went out onto the road and began to drive, did you know what you were going to do that day?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We were driving. You mean where we were driving to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you know why you and your neighbours had been ordered to get their trucks and to drive along the road to Malisevo? Did you know why you were told to do that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. To go and fetch refugees from Malisheva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you know where you were going to bring those refugees?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: To the -- to Pirana and then -- then Shipka told us to go on to Rahovec and in that direction, so we set off in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before you got to Malisevo, did you know what you were going to do with the refugees who you were going to pick up there?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. We knew that we were going to fetch them and take them to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, how did you know that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: The police told us. "You've got to go and fetch refugees and take them to Albania."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you got to Malisevo and you saw this large crowd of refugees there, did any of the refugees there tell you what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No, they didn't. The refugees told us nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When the refugees boarded your truck in Malisevo, did you ask any of them whether they wanted to go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They got in, but we didn't talk to them. They -- we just closed the trucks and they told us, "Set off for the border."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why didn't you ask any of the refugees if they wanted to go to Albania or not?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: We were afraid for our own sakes as well, quite apart from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe how the refugees looked who boarded your truck? Were they happy, laughing?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. They were weeping. They were -- they were very, very upset.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you arrived at the village of Zur and you stopped the truck and you asked the refugees in your truck whether they could walk to the border and the refugees got down from the truck, were the refugees -- how could you describe the refugees at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They were all weeping. And then we embraced them and we said, "Safe journey. God help you." And there was nothing else we could do, and then we went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just one last question. You remarked that your village was quiet between the 24th of March and the 2nd of April. By the word "quiet," do you mean no conflict, no armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: There was no armed conflict apart from on the 27th, but we didn't have any conflicts of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the night of the 27th, you described how houses were burning. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: A few minutes ago, you said that the persons who died that evening died from gunfire. Do you know -- do you have personal knowledge whether those persons died from the flames in their homes or from gunfire or both, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: They weren't burned. They died from bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, have you ever said to the investigator or the Prosecution that you cried as you saw the refugee people getting on your trucks?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I cried too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why did you cry?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Because I felt sorry for these brothers of mine. Where were they going? What would happen to them? It pained me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, you have told us that the journey from Malisevo to Zur took about two hours.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For most of that time, you and the refugees were entirely on your own. There was no police escort, no army escort. Did it not occur to you that you might have been able to escape, you might have deviated, you might have directed from the course and not go straight on to Zur and ultimately to Albania?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. I never thought of anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Well, they told us to send them to the border. That's what the police said. There was nowhere else we could take them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the refugees themselves said to you to set off to the border; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: The refugees didn't say this. The police said this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me try the transcript. Just awhile ago you said that the refugees, "They got in but we didn't talk to them. They -- we just closed the trucks and they told us, `Set off for the border,'" while Mr. Saxon asked you questions.

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who are "they" --

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the refugees said to you to set off for the border?

utterances.speaker: SAKIR TAC
utterances.text: No. The refugees didn't say this. It was the police and the army who told us to take these people straight to the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tac, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The statement will be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 52.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And I shall ask the legal officer to have the translation clarified of the third paragraph in the statement, which is not clear and is obviously important; it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If it please the Court, I propose to call the next witness, Mr. Hazbi Loku. While we're waiting for the witness to come in, I will be proposing to show the witness a bundle of documents. In order to save time, I wonder whether we can have those distributed in advance so that I can ask the usher to present them to the witness in order. The summary should give an indication as to about when I propose to do that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would the registrar please assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, I understand, sir, that you are 41 years old and that your ethnicity is Albanian, a Kosovo Albanian, and you are from the village of Kotlina in the municipality of Kacanik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do I also understand correctly, sir, that you are presently married and with four children?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And by way of background, very briefly, you attended the Skopje Teaching Academy in Macedonia while you were teaching, and you became a teacher in 1981; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And then, sir, I understand you became the primary school principal of the village of Kotlina in 1994.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, at the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could I ask you to show the witness what has been entered in these proceedings as Exhibit 3, map 12.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness draw closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, could you come closer to the microphone so the interpreters can hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Usher, if you could show that to the witness first, and then once he's had a look at it, we can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you see the map there, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now it's going on the overhead projector. I'm going to ask you to take the pointer, if there is one in front of you -- there you go. And could you point out where, approximately, your village of Kotlina would be on this map if you see it there.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The village is not marked on this map, but I think I can show you where it is because I grew up there. There it is, about there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. You're pointing now, just for the record, to what appears to be a pink sort of mark underneath the "A" of "Ivaja" and above the "O" of -- the second "O" of "Globocica"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how far would you say that is from Ivaja, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Our village is a neighbouring village to Ivaja. About four kilometres away. We're a next-door village, centre-to-centre about four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might be the witness now be shown, please, a new map. That's part of the package that I've just provided. I might say, Your Honours, this will be the first of a series of maps from the second portion of the indictment. You will note that we have been talking about deportation sites and you have a bundle of maps for that. This will be one of a bundle of maps which we anticipate presenting under the killing sites, and I'm in Your Honours' hands as to how we want to deal with them. Do we want to deal with them separately like this or would you eventually like us to have, as we did with Exhibit 3, have the exhibit with maps numbered? Because we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The latter course is more convenient --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I thought it may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- if they're kept together, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The trouble is, of course, with the previous bundle I was able to put them in through Mr. Spargo, but we didn't get these maps put in as a bundle through Mr. Curtis. So we'll find another way to do that, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. They'll need some sort of number meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. I propose that we simply call this then Exhibit 53, map 1, and we'll sort it out from there. Am I right about that, Madam Clerk?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 53, map 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Might the witness be shown this map. That can go straight on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just have a look at it, Witness. Do you see your village of Kotlina marked on this particular map?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Could you use that pointer, please, and tell the Court where that is.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The village is here, my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. And that's sort of a star where it's marked "Kotlina," and there's two --

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And do you see Ivaja to the north of that?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, in the north. In the west is Gllobocica. The west [sic], Lac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, sir, is it also correct that you did your normal Serb compulsory military service in the JNA when you were 21 years old, in 1980?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. During 1980, 1981 I did my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what -- was there a particular unit that you were attached to at that time?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: You think during my military service?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. I was doing my military police service in the former Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, I'd like you to turn your mind to the month, the early part of the month of March 1999. We're skipping right to there. You've been asked and you've pointed out the village of Ivaja on the map, and you've indicated that that was a neighbouring village. Did something happen in respect to the neighbouring villages, including Ivaja, on or about the 8th of March that you can recall and tell us about today?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: In the morning of 8th of March of 1999, in the vicinity around my village and the adjacent villages, we could feel the shells dropping by and explosions. We could see that something was going on there. The population were anxious to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did they?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. The firing never stopped during all the day. After the shelling, there were other shots coming from different arms. This lasted for three days. We heard the noise in the village. We were afraid, and we took shelter in a place at the end of village, even though there too we didn't feel very safe. But out of fear, we couldn't stay at home. So we felt safer there than at home. And we wanted to see what we should do under the circumstances. There was panic prevailing all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just stop there, if you would, please, sir. I want to back up a little bit. You're jumping ahead of us. You've talked about the 8th of March first, and you've told us that you could hear shelling. Did you at some point --

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- go to the neighbouring village of Ivaja to find out for yourself what had happened?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I went to the neighbouring village of Ivaja at a later phase, two or three days after the 8th of March. I think it was 11th or 12th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And when you got there, what, if anything, did you see?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: You think [as interpreted] in Ivaja?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Absolutely. You've just told us you went there. Now I'm asking: When you went there, i.e. Ivaja, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: When I arrived in Ivaja, I saw houses destroyed, burned. Some of them were still in flames and smoke. Some were ruined because of the tanks that had passed through the village streets. I saw the village mosque also destroyed and ruined. I saw cattle dead, lying on the streets. I saw that half the school building was ruined and burned. This is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not -- what you noted about the mosque, what of the mosque was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The mosque was destroyed and burned, the building and the roof, the minaret. The minaret was also destroyed. It was half destroyed. It had capsized.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, before we leave the village of Ivaja in our description of events, I'm going to ask you what, if anything, you knew of why it was that the village of Ivaja may have been the subject of this shelling.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Around the village of Ivaja, there were the KLA troops, those who tried to protect the population from the worse that might befall them, and I think that the residents of that village managed to escape the worst.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've told us that you went back a few days later, but I'm going to now try to deal with the time period in between. You've told us about hearing the shelling on the 8th, you've told us about seeing the results of that shelling on the 11th or 12th. I now want to direct your mind to the 9th of March, that is, the following day after having heard the shelling. What, if anything, happened to your village?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The same thing happened, also in the morning. We heard shells dropping in my village. Shells were coming from a distance. We could see the Serb positions from which the grenades -- the shells came, in a place called Kashan, and from that place our village was very visible, most of it, at least. So the shells came from that direction as well as from the east, the north. The same anxiety prevailed. People didn't know what to do. They didn't know if they were attacked from one side or if something worse was going to happen to them, if the troops were coming to the village. So some younger people who were braver than the others, they went out to see what was happening. There are two roads, one leading to Kacanik, the other to Globocica, and the population wanted to run away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Why did they want to run away? What were they afraid of?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: They were afraid of the Serb military forces, because some months ago we were seeing what was happening all over Kosova, and in those places where the population was defenceless, everybody knew what they fared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, it's 1.00. Is that a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. Mr. Loku, would you remember in this adjournment and any other there may be while you're giving evidence not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that includes members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, at half past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, just before the lunch break, I had directed your mind to the incidents in your village on the 9th of March, and I believe you had just told us that -- words to the effect that people of your village were deciding that they were going to leave. Can you pick it up from there, please, and tell us -- you told us, I think, that younger men went to go and scout out to find out what was happening. Did they come back and report?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them returned to the village, those who had been on the road to Kacanik. They returned and reported that Serbian forces were coming from that direction and the road was blocked. They said that they had been shot at by the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: As a result of that information, what, if anything, did you and/or the rest of the villagers decide to do?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The entire population, we were all on the village street, and seeing that it was blocked on that side, we decided to set off in the direction of the border towards the village of Gllobocica, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So -- I think you told us earlier there were two roads. One road was blocked and the other road that was open was the one to the border; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. At that moment that road was open, so the population headed towards Gllobocica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The population, including women, children, and the elderly, headed for the border. And we knew that the entrance to Gllobocica was being patrolled by Serbian forces, so we younger people, that is men from 17 to 50, were scared because we were sure that they would divide us from our families. So we thought it would be safer for us if we went into hiding round the village. So we separately - and we didn't go with them - the women, children, and the elderly went on, and elderly people, women, and children carried the ill.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you find out whether or not they were able to go all the way or did something stop them from going all the way?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Those of us who had scattered or, rather, had hidden in the vicinity of the village - and we thought that we had found a safer place - still kept watch of the road towards Gllobocica to see whether our women and families would be able to pass. And I saw with my own eyes from the place where I was hiding that the women, as they approached a neighbourhood called Dreshec, which they had to pass through to get to the border, were shot at by a hail of bullets from Serbian forces which were in Gllobocica. You could see this neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just finish your sentence. You could see the neighbourhood, yes. You could see this neighbourhood from your hiding place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You could see that neighbourhood. I could see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, you've told us --

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I would see the people being stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. You told us -- you used the expression "Serb forces." When you say that, what kinds of Serb forces did you see?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I saw tanks, Serbian tanks. I saw the Serbian army and the Serbian police. These were the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were they separate or were they together or were they all in this neighbourhood of Dreshec, or what can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The Serbian forces, after stopping the population and not allowing them to proceed to Gllobocica, the populous no doubt knew that they were drawing near, and so they went off and hid in the neighbourhood. And half an hour later, tanks made their presence felt in that neighbourhood and could be seen from a distance. And we saw police and soldiers starting to raid that neighbourhood. Although it was empty and didn't have anybody living in it, they started to loot and to burn that neighbourhood as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Can I ask you to stop there, sir. You're just slightly ahead of where I wanted to be. You've told us about the women and the children and the elderly being stopped by Serb forces. You went on to explain that that was tanks, the army and police. I'm going to ask you, if you would, please: When you say "army" and "police," I'm going to ask you to look at Exhibit 18 and tell us whether any of the uniforms of the army and police you saw are depicted in Exhibit 18, and if so, which photographs? Again, use the pointer, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Could we show this on the ELMO now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: First of all, the soldiers. Did you see what uniforms, if any, they were wearing, and if so, what is the closest on Exhibit 18? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The soldiers were wearing uniforms of this colour, more or less green, with lines on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And for the record, you're now pointing at Exhibit 18, photograph number 9; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you see any other uniforms there, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. There were also police uniforms, dark blue with stripes, mainly blue, number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Number 6. Thank you very much. Thank you. Sir, I interrupted you at a point when you said that you also saw tanks and you saw looting and houses being damaged. Could you pick it up from there and tell us: Was that still the same day, the 9th of March, that you saw this?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, it was on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Tell us what you saw.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: In this neighbourhood, the police and the army started to act together and went among the houses, and shortly afterwards, smoke rose. They were looting, taking things that they fancied. This was only a neighbourhood of the village of Kotlina. And then the same forces headed for the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. Just so that we're very clear, this neighbourhood that you're now talking about, was that the same neighbourhood of Dreshec that you mentioned earlier or a different neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: It's the same neighbourhood of Dreshec. That was completely burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we can follow, this is all Kotlina, not Globocica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask the witness that, but that's my understanding, yes. It's a neighbourhood of Kotlina on the way to Globocica, is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Have I got that right, Witness, that Dreshec is a neighbourhood of your village of Kotlina, and that's the direction that you would take leaving Kotlina to go towards Globocica?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Now, once you saw what happened in Dreshec, the neighbourhood of Kotlina, you said they went towards the centre of town. What town are we talking about? Is that Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. They went on to the centre of the village, to the main part of the village where the school is and the shops. In the village centre, other forces had arrived from the direction of Ivaja, and they had been looting everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you say "other forces," do you know what kind of forces we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Forces that had entered the centre of the village. I was unable to see them, but I could see them moving towards the village, because I was in hiding and could only see the neighbourhood being looted and burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you know -- well, all right. Just continue on. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Throughout the day, there were incessant gunshots, so before dusk they stopped and we gradually went back towards the village to see what had been happening. We went back to the village and, at the same time, our families, women and children, followed us and we saw everything destroyed: Doors burned, windows broken. There was a shop near the road which had been run down by tanks as they went through the village. There was no electricity. And indeed, even before the offensive, we had had no electricity. It was terrible. Everybody was looking for their nearest and dearest. We waited all night for people to come back, people who had fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were there any missing? I'm sorry to have asked you that, Witness, but I have to ask it.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, people were missing. The next morning, the OSCE came to the village with -- this was on the 10th of March in the morning. That was when they came. We -- we all realised that they had been there. And Milaim Loku, my brother, was one of the missing. And another villager called Emrlah Kuqi. They didn't come back. And we asked the OSCE to find out whether the Serbian forces had captured them or taken them with them or something like that. But nevertheless, a few days later, they didn't know anything about them and they hadn't been taken prisoner. So I and others started to search round the village, thinking that we might find them. Maybe they had been killed, because they just didn't turn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you in fact find them?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. In the course of our search, after six days, I found my own brother. He had been killed. He was in the village stream.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Can the witness be given a Kleenex, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would you like a glass of water, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you go on, Mr. Loku, or would you like a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn for five minutes. --- Break taken at 2.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you all right now, Mr. Loku? Are you able to go on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, sir, let's move on to another topic then. I think you told us that on the 10th of March, the OSCE arrived. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how long did they stay?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: They stayed in the village until the 23rd, if I'm not mistaken. The 23rd of March. Yes, it was the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And during that period of time, sir, what generally were the conditions in your village?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: During this period, we all felt safe. We stayed in the village. We slept better. Even though there was no electricity, they came with their cars to the village at night and kept their headlights on so that there was light in the village so that we could sleep in peace with our children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And to your recollection, they left on the 23rd of March; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did something happen the next day, the 24th of March, to your village?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, something did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Tell us about that, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: On the morning of that day, the village was subjected to shelling. There was panic again among the population. Most of the villagers thought that the OSCE would come back. They didn't realise that they had gone, not to come back. We realised that shooting had started.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you say "shooting started," where was the shooting coming from and what kind of shooting are you talking about? Are you talking about gunfire or shelling from some other source?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The village is situated in a deep valley. It's a mountain village, and about 150 metres above the village, above the school, a tank appeared. We saw the tank drawing near to the village. And after it, soldiers and policemen were coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How long did the shelling go on?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The shelling didn't last long. From dawn, at about 6.00 until 7.00, they didn't fall on the village but around the village. And then the shelling stopped, and they started firing from the tank. Not from the barrel of the tank but from weapons that were positioned on top of the tank and other forms of gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And where were those shots being directed at?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: These shots were directed at the direction of the houses of the village, that is, they hit above the houses. There is a great stone in the village, and they shot at this stone, around the village in order to strike terror in the people. Then when we had lost hopes in the return of the OSCE monitors and we could hear the approaching tanks, all the young people who were scared to stay on had left the village because they wanted to escape to a better and safer place. Whoever managed to leave, left. A cousin of mine and myself, we were separated from our families and went to the southern part of the village. Most of the people had left from that way. It was a deep stream running by. We stopped at that stream. There was a hill and a mountain there. We stopped there to see what was happening. It was very late.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there for a moment. We'll get back to that point. When the shelling on your village happened, did you see any return gunfire come from the village back towards the people that were attacking? In other words, did the villagers shoot back?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: No, the villagers didn't shoot back. Not a single shot was fired by the villagers. We all knew that the villagers didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. I'll take you back, then, to the point where you and a cousin went into hiding, I think you said on the south part of the village; is that right, or did I get that wrong?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. We went to the southern part of the village. There is a raised hill there from where you can see most of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And from that vantage point, sir, what did you see? Tell the Court what you saw.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: From that vantage point, we saw the police and the military forces that had surrounded the village, mostly from the northern part. They not only fired from the tank, but they had spread out in the village and were approaching while they were firing all the time. So some of the houses that were on a higher place near the mountain, I saw in those houses some young people who, because of the fear of the fire spreading up, they were approaching these houses. They were about 50 metres away from these houses, but they didn't make it to the houses because they were captured by the Serbian forces. They were gathered in a meadow near the house, and there they were kept, surrounded. They were mistreated and they were told to tie their hands behind their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you see any elderly men or women or children?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What, from your vantage point, did you see them doing?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The Serb police and army together, they acted together, in concert. So they entered every house and ransacked them, driving the inhabitants out, although in the meantime most of the inhabitants had already left their houses and had gathered in the centre of the village. The police and the soldiers who were there, they separated the elderly people from the wives and the children. They told them to lie on the ground with their face down, and the women and children were separate. They searched the women and the children and took away whatever valuable possessions they had on them. They went in and out of every house. Even those people who had not yet left their houses, they asked them to leave. And so this went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. I'm going to stop you there to get a couple of details, if I can. We'll continue with the narrative in a moment. You've told us that you had seen a tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you show the witness Exhibit 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Exhibit 17, sir, are four pages of what appear to be vehicles. Would you quickly look through all four pages and tell us whether or not any of the vehicles that you saw that you call tanks are depicted in any of the photographs comprising Exhibit 17. Just look at them all first and then tell us if there are any.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. The tank is here. This is what I saw that day, number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The tanks were of this type that I see here, number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. How many tanks did you see from your hiding place?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: From my hiding place, I saw one of the tanks stopping above the village, the others continuing their way towards the village. The village was -- the road was curved. Two or three, I think, continued their way towards the village and entered the school yard. Apart from the tanks --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: -- there were also armoured cars. I don't know what their name is. Pinzgauers, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you see any vehicles in the selection of photographs comprising Exhibit 17 - that's four separate pages - that you would call Pinzgauers?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. This type here, number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how many of those did you see?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Number 7. This kind. There were two or three. There was also another type.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Shuffle through the photographs and tell us if you see the other type you want to tell us about.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. Of this here, number 1, this type. They were large like tanks, almost the same, but they didn't have long barrels.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And these were all together, the tanks and the Pinzgauers and these vehicles that look like photograph 1 of Exhibit 17, they were all together on the 24th of March, near your village?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Let's move on, sir. You were then about to tell us, or you did start telling us about the men and the women and the children being separated and the men being told to put their hands behind their necks. The people that were telling them to do that, did you see what they were dressed like, in other words, the Serb forces? What kinds of Serb forces did you see?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And perhaps Exhibit 18 may be of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: First of all, tell us what you can recall, sir. Were there police?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: There were police and army forces together.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How did you know there were police there? Was there any insignia telling you that they were police?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The army forces had green uniforms with some stripes. The police had blue uniforms with some stripes but with blue predominating. And on the back they had "militia" written.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, did you see some elderly men at any point from your observation?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. From my vantage point, I could see the women and the children staying in the middle. They were closer to the place I was hiding, and I could see better. There weren't many men. About 20 of them, I think. Elderly men who had remained with the women. I saw all of them were lying down face down. They were surrounded by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you know any of these elderly men by name?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. I knew each and every one of them. They took Idriz Kuqi. He was about 55 years of age. He was wearing a white fez hat. And then they headed him towards the mosque of the village, and he never returned any more to the group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I hesitate to ask this but I'm going to anyway, sir: Did you subsequently see Idriz Kuqi later, after this incident?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Where and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: After the occupation, Serb forces left. Idriz Kuqi's body was found in the yard of the house of Liman Loku. He was shot dead in his yard near the toilet. He was shot in the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, just before I leave this area, sir, and move on, from your hiding place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just see -- did you see that body yourself, Mr. Loku?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did somebody tell you about seeing his body or did you personally see the body?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Idriz Kuqi's body, I saw it with my own eyes. And not only his body, but also I saw other bodies, dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, just backing up for a moment, when you were watching what was happening to the villagers from your hiding place, you were able to see that with your naked eye, were you?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. All the time I saw it with my naked eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you have anything else with you that enabled you to see better?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: My cousin and I who were there, we had binoculars that we used for shooting, for hunting, and they helped us to see better what was going on. The vantage point wasn't that far, so it enabled us to see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, I've asked you about the men, the elderly men, and you said that Idriz Kuqi was taken away. What, if anything, did you see happening to the women and children?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The women and children, as I said, they were surrounded by the Serb forces. Then at -- about two or three, I think. Two trucks came from the direction of Lac, a lower direction, and they boarded the women and the children on these two trucks. The others who couldn't get on because there was no more room, they asked them to follow the trucks on foot, threatening them always with their arms butts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
