utterances.text: When you say "with their arms," you don't mean the arms sticking Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. out of their bodies, you mean weapons when you say "arms" or --?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: No. I mean the police who were keeping the crowd of women and children at gunpoint and following them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. That's what you mean by "arms." All right. How many women and children would you say were gathered of whom two lorry loads were able to be taken away? How many were there?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I would say approximately 400 of them, because ours is a small village. We are about 500 people. One hundred were males. The others were women and children. Three hundred fifty, I would say, 400.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, these two lorries full of people followed by the rest of them on foot, which direction did they go?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: They went in the direction of Lac village, Kashan, in the direction of Kacanik. This is where that road leads to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And do you know if villagers were driving those military trucks or was someone else driving those trucks? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do you know who were driving the trucks? Was it the villagers?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The trucks belonged to the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, after those trucks left, what, if anything, happened to the men that had been captured and not taken with the other villagers?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Those who were taken earlier in the forest nearby after the population left, these people, with their hands behind their necks, in a line, were taken to the mountain overlooking the village. They were taken to the mountain. They brought them near two big holes. They had dug two big holes, because the villagers some years ago had dug for water there, and they were still there, dry but very deep.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I realise this is a very painful matter for you to have to recount, sir, but I'm going to ask you to do your best, please.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: There were about 20 people that were being led towards this forest. Most of them were young. They brought them to these holes. Certainly they didn't know what was going to happen to them. The first who came to the holes, they threw them into it, three or four, I think. Then everything happened. It was a nightmare.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I could hear the shrieks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, just try and tell us, if you can, what happened. You saw all this, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I saw everything with my naked eye. I could hear their voices, screaming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were maltreated in various forms and ways. Some of them were begging, hoping that they would let them go. After half an hour, every one of them was thrown in the holes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did something happen shortly after they were all thrown into these holes?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: After that, the police returned to the village. At the same time, I saw the houses going on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Just before you saw that happen, sir, we've got these boys or men being thrown into the holes. Did you see anything else in relation to the holes after the men were thrown into it? Did something happen shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, it did, but a little while later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. All right.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I was all the time seeing the houses in flames, and then afterwards I heard a very powerful explosion, and from these holes I saw smoke coming up, which then I understood that nothing was left of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm just going to show you a couple of photographs at this point, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown what has been marked, I believe, as reference number K1040A. Show it to the witness, please, before you put it. All right. Now that you've seen the photograph, sir, could we put that on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've told us that the village of Kotlina, that there was a mountainside with two holes. Looking at this photograph, what can you tell us? Is that the village of Kotlina we're looking at in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, that's the village itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There appears to be a mountain in the background, and there is superimposed a red arrow pointing to what appears to be a -- well, a hole in the trees there. What can you tell us about that? Are those the holes?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown a photograph of K --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Are we at 54?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The next will be this photograph, Your Honours, and the reference number is K2271.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They look to be, on the photograph, they look like caves, in fact, but is that wrong? Am I looking at it the wrong way?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The witness can explain what these are, Your Honour. They were, as I understand it, well holes that had been dug. Then we have an explosion, which enlarged them. This would be after the explosion, of course. This is a photograph the witness brought with him, so we'll have him explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would you look at this photograph, please, sir, Exhibit 55. Did you bring a smaller copy of that photograph with you from your village of Kotlina when you came to testify?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is this an enlargement of the photograph you personally brought?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: His Honour asked whether or not these are caves, or what can you tell us about these holes? I believe you told us earlier they were dug by someone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They were dug to find water, because they're above the level of the village and they were to carry water to the houses. But the villager was unable to find water and they were just left as they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that these young men, about 20 of them or so, were thrown into these holes?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it with my own eyes. They were all thrown in these holes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can he say how deep these holes were?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, have you seen these holes after the explosion?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: No, I didn't myself go to the holes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you know how deep those holes were before the young men were thrown in? Had you ever looked at those holes before to see how deep they were?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know. I never saw them either before or afterwards. I know that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I propose to move on and then return to the final issue, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, these young men that you saw being thrown into these holes, were any of them KLA members, to your knowledge, or any of them combatants, or were they civilians? Are you able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: They were all civilians from the village. Among them there were three high school pupils. They were caught as they were escaping from their houses to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'll get back to those people in a moment. You told us that at about the same time as you saw these bodies being thrown into the holes, you saw houses being burned in the village. Now, did the Serb troops and police eventually leave the village of Kotlina that day?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. Late in the evening when darkness had fallen, they withdrew, leaving the village in flames. All the houses were on fire, all the cow sheds; everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you and some of the other villagers who had gone into hiding try to do something in relation to the animals?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. After the Serbian army and police withdrew, my cousin and I went straight back to the houses because you could hear the screams of animals being burned alive. And others also went back to look for the members of their families among the houses. They didn't find anything, but they freed some animals. And so we gathered in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In the course of trying to free animals that were trapped in buildings, did you find any other villagers who had not survived?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. When I was -- I was in the yard looking at the body of Idriz Kuqi in the house of Liman Loku, it was a two-story house on fire. One other villager found the lifeless body of Vesel Vlashi, also an elderly man. He had been a cleaner at the school. He had been a member of my staff. He -- he was dead and his body was starting to burn. And they pulled him out into the yard and left the two of them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I might direct Your Honours' attention at this point to Schedule L. The first name and last name in Schedule L have just been referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was there a third person who was found and who later died, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was elderly man, 70 years old. His name was Zymer Loku. He was found seriously wounded with his right leg cut off and bullets in his body. It was in vain to give him help, and he died shortly after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Schedule L, fourth name from the bottom of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Moving on if, I may, because I'd like to finish in ten minutes if I can, sir. I understand that after seeing all this happening, later that evening you left Kotlina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. After all that horror, all that burning, I didn't know where my family was, whether they had been killed or what had happened to them. We didn't know what to do. We others decided to leave the village, and we walked all night and crossed the border into Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How many of you had remained behind and how many of you left that night for Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: There were about 50 of us who had gathered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you in fact did get to the Macedonia border by walking all night, the next morning. Where did you cross the border?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: We passed the border during the night of the 24th, 25th of March, towards 6.00 in the morning when we entered the village of Jazhinca, which is on the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. Usher, if we could show the witness Exhibit 3, map 12 again. And while that's coming out, I'm going to ask a couple more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, while you were in Macedonia, did you meet up with other villagers from Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. We were all in Skopje or Tetovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you find out what happened to those men who had been thrown into the holes, apart from what you saw?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: On that night when we set off to cross the border, three elderly people remained in the village. Rexhep Loku had three missing sons. Zymer Loku, who was also missing a son. And Damir Kuqi, who also was handicapped and couldn't walk. They remained behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, look at the map, if you would, please. You've looked at this map before. For the record, Exhibit 3, map 12. Is the route you took walking out from Kotlina, is that on this map? There are some blue lines with arrows. Is your route depicted in this map?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The blue path from Kotlina to Gllobocica is the route whereby the population, the women and the children, tried to go. And the road by which I and others passed -- crossed the border, got through Goranca, and we came out a different place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And the route that the women and children took, is that shown on this map?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, it is shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you -- I'm sorry. Maybe I misunderstood what you said. Could you, with your pointer, show the Court which route that the women and children took when they were driven away in those two lorries?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The children -- no. Now I'm talking about 9th of March when the women tried to go to Gllobocica. But on the 24th, they went on the road through Lac and up to Kacanik. Here on the right is the road they followed on the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And the route you personally took on the evening of the -- I guess it was the 24th of March and the early morning of the 25th of March, was that directly to the Macedonian border? Is that shown? You may have answered this, and I may not have understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: We, rather, went through the mountains, not on the roads. We crossed the border illegally, in some danger. And we don't know how we got through, but we went through the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Just a couple more quick questions, sir. To your knowledge, was your village ever bombed by NATO?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: No. No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that your village was bombed by NATO?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: No. After we reached Jazhinca - it was the morning of the 25th of March - they told us that NATO had intervened in Kosova, and we were so pleased. And we thought if they had intervened earlier, perhaps these people would have been saved. We were pleased that NATO had intervened, because we knew that many other people were in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, eventually you left Macedonia and you returned to your village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. I returned to the village --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And when you got there --

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: -- towards the middle of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. When you got there, what can you tell us about the condition of the village you returned to? What did it look like to you? And I have some photographs you brought with you to show you.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: When we returned to the village, the village was destroyed, just as we had left it that night. Everything was devastated and burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, you brought some photographs with you to The Hague; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, I'm going to interrupt. We have to have this argument tonight. We can't sit beyond half past 4.00. Would it be convenient to deal with the photographs in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Certainly. We could do that, because I have some other photographs to deal with as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. I probably would take another five to ten minutes to complete this, and this might be the best time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to adjourn now. Mr. Loku, would you be back, please, tomorrow morning, to conclude your evidence, at half past 9.00. We'll adjourn for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. --- Break taken at 3.43 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we've just been handed, as we came in, an additional document, an additional response. I should say that we've read all the pleadings on this issue to date and, having had them in writing, we must ask everybody to be brief in oral submissions, at least you and the amicus. With that in mind, you've each got ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. The latest document, which is filed today and for which courtesy copies have been provided, explains one or two substitutions of names for names and in its schedule brings the earlier schedule up to date. If I can invite the Chamber to look at the schedule briefly, it will see what has been set out there is the following: In the left-hand box -- I'm sorry. These have not found their way yet to the interpreters' booths. If there are some further copies, may they be provided straight away. And until they come, I'll speak even more slowly than I always do. The left-hand box contains facts that may be described as the highest common factor of the statements viva voce or proposed via 92 bis and listed on the right-hand side. And so what is true for what is set out in Orahovac or Rahovec is also true for Prizren, and so on. Your Honour, with that pattern in mind, I need deal no further with the document beyond saying this: As the Chamber may know, I think a second mission to complete the attestations required for 92 bis statements is under way at the moment, and of course further statements will become available should they be admitted in due course and will have to be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. subject to further applications pending the outcome of this hearing today. The Chamber is, I hope, assisted by not only the amici's brief but our now two documents, and I don't desire to repeat anything said there, but simply to make the following general and, I hope, helpful observations to guide the Chamber in what we venture to suggest will be a difficult task for this Chamber to perform. There is a hierarchy in the form of evidence that comes before this Chamber, each of which form of evidence may attract different weight and take different amounts of time to be given. At the top of the hierarchy, of course, is evidence given by full examination-in-chief, followed by the fullest of cross-examination. Second, if it should ever become necessary to consider it, is evidence where the evidence in chief can be given by adoption of a signed summary in order to save time, followed by full cross-examination. It's not something I think that's been tried very much or at all here, but given the tension between proper length of trial and proper examination of evidence, it's something that we might all want to have in mind as a reserve possibility. Third in the hierarchy, if we allow for that second alternative, is the 92 bis proposal, and of course 92 bis statements, even if read or summarised to the Court, save an enormous amount of court time. Finally, there may be before the Chamber in one form or another statements read or summarised by others, for example, in the OSCE reports of the kind that the accused has been cross-examining on, human rights reports, and others. And indeed, the Chamber knows it was the Prosecution's proposal to summarise evidence by its own investigators' reports, a matter to which we would have invited the Chamber in due course to return. The timetable for this trial was fixed by the Trial Chamber without particular input or discussion from the Prosecution but with regard, no doubt, to the estimates of time that the Prosecution gave to the evidence it would lead. Those estimates, however, were made on the basis of expected non- or low participation by the accused, and it may be inevitable that the present timetable may have to yield to change given, one, that the estimates were based effectively on no cross-examination, which at least doubles the time each witness takes; and two, that the very proper involvement of the accused in the trial is resulting in the raising of issues which may both extend evidence to be given viva voce or indeed add to the evidence which must be led to deal with the matters the accused raises. I have to make it plain that this Prosecution is willing to have as much evidence led as -- live as is possible, and indeed I must inform the Chamber that witnesses generally are anxious to give evidence live and typically unhappy to learn that their evidence may be given simply in the form of any written statement. But with all that background in mind, it is our duty to provide the Chamber with every means possible expediting the trial. We take the view that the Trial Chamber could properly adopt an inclusive approach and to decide the issues about 92 bis statements with an inclusive approach in mind. And I refer back not only to the various hierarchies of evidence but in particular to the possibility that in due course, particularly when it's heard OSCE witnesses or indeed when it's considered Dr. Ball's report tomorrow, it may conclude that some attention to the analysis of witnesses by others is desirable and appropriate, both because those reports of others have weight in themselves, enable a Trial Chamber to check its tentative conclusions against other material, and also because that other material will assist the Chamber to decide where and when it needs to look further for evidence. And so those are the background matters and the approach we invite the Chamber to take. And with all those matters in mind and because I'm not going to repeat what is set out in our briefs or in the schedule to the brief, we invite the Chamber to say that all these statements that have been listed, whatever it is, 31 so far but with more to come, properly fall within the present 92 bis Rule which permits admission in whole or in part the evidence of a witness which goes to proof of a matter other than the acts of the accused as charged in the indictment, and that by doing so, this will assist in the fair determination of issues without in any sense diminishing the fairness of the trial. We repeat that we are entirely content to call any or all of these witnesses if the Chamber, in the difficult decision and discretion it has to make and exercise decides that that should be the case, but we would say that should such other witnesses be called live, that should in no way be at the expense of any of the time otherwise available for other parts of our evidence which still require the time originally contemplated for them and indeed may, for the reasons I've already given, require more time. So, Your Honours, in summary, those are our submissions on 92 bis and I don't know if I can help you further certainly at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Trial Chamber noticed that the amici filed a brief in order to seek guidance on the issue to assist the accused to make up his mind on the issue itself. Now, let me start to say that we perfectly well understand the idea of the Prosecution to seek the filing of the statements. It has been said a minute ago again. If such filing is necessary, it will certainly speed up things. And having said this, it seems to the amici that the first test here is the necessity of the offer of the Prosecution to file statements instead of live evidence in court. The criterion of necessity raises an issue with the positive factor (a) listed in paragraph (i) of section (a) of Rule 92 bis. The Rules at least consider (i) to be a positive factor when the written statement is of a cumulative nature in that other witnesses have given live testimony of similar facts. This, of course, could or would conflict with the criterion of necessity. A sensible approach seems this: If live evidence is capable to prove the issue at hand, the question raises whether further evidence is necessary. If the Trial Chamber is satisfied with the oral evidence so far, the test of necessity is not met. The second issue is the concern of the amici about parts of hearsay evidence in the written statements. Here we reiterate that the written statements were not given under judicial supervision and that the reliability is not tested. The role of the Presiding Officer does not cover this matter. The use of written statements is not unique. In other jurisdictions, like in civil law systems, it's daily practice. But in those systems, Judges make a distinction between statements taken by investigators and those taken under judicial control, that is, in most cases by an investigating Judge. When the Trial Chamber, being professional Judges, does not see an obstacle here and therefore accepts the filing of written statements, the amici respectfully suggests to the Trial Chamber not to consider those parts of the statement that passes hearsay evidence. The third issue is the right of the accused, under paragraph (e) of section 4 of Article 21, the right to examine the witnesses against him. This indeed, Your Honours, is a crucial basic right of an accused. The Statute does say -- does not say anything about limitation and circumstances, so the question is whether this right is absolute. In the Aleksovski case, the Trial Chamber held that the exercise of the defendant's fair trial rights may, depending on the circumstances, be tempered by other concerns such as the need for equality between the parties. It seems not necessary to examine all the ins and outs of all the fair trial rights. Here we are dealing with the right of the accused to examine witnesses against him for the very reason that the accused should, in this respect, be equal to the Prosecution. This is a one-way equality and not, as the Prosecution seems to interpret in their brief, a vice versa equality. The fair trial rights in the Statute are meant to provide the accused and no one else a fair trial. Leaving aside the general assertion of the Prosecution that they are entitled to fair trial rights as well, we believe that this is not the issue here from the perspective of the Prosecution. Their rights to cross-examine witnesses are not at stake. Whatever is the case, it is unlikely that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence can simply override the basic rights of this basic right of the Statute. This understanding of Article 21 of the Statute in relation to the Rules is, in my opinion, one of the leading principles of the decision of your Trial Chamber, though in a slightly different composition, in the Sikirica case, as cited in our brief. So the reasoning of Rule 92 bis may derive from a perspective that does not conflict with the rights of the accused under the Statute. The factors as listed under paragraph (i) under section (A) of Rule 92 bis may be such a perspective. Now, what if such factors conflict to each other? This seems to be the case in the present case since the accused objected to the use of written statements. This objection is a negative factor as listed under (b) of paragraph (ii) of section (A) of Rule 92 bis. The applicability of this negative factor, however, may depend on a proper showing or demonstration on the part of the accused that either the nature or source of his statements are unreliable or that its prejudicial effect outweighs its probative nature. The amici, Your Honours, are not in the position to argue this factor simply because we are not in any way instructed. The accused, however, did so far not specifically -- did not specifically give any thought to the issue. I can only say that on one hand there seems not to be a prima facie case for one of these arguments as raised in the Rule itself, but on the other hand, we have heard the challenges of the accused to the evidence given by live witnesses on the issues covered in the written -- in the written statements. Balancing these interests, the amici suggests for the reasons of consistency that in that case of conflict, the negative factors override the positive ones, and this would result in not accepting the filing of the written statements. That brings me to the fourth issue, whether the substantive nature of the information contained in the written statement would potentially constitute proof of a critical element of the Prosecution's case. The Prosecution is right when it argues that proof of the crime base does not go to the acts and conduct of the accused himself, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff is kindly requested to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. But those facts presented in the written statements, however, do indirectly go to the matters that are linked in the indictment to acts and conduct of the accused. That is a matter for your Trial Chamber to consider. Different to the Prosecution arguing a broad interpretation of the term "critical element," the amici believe that such interpretation would be inconsistent with the fair trial rights of the Statute. It would turn the right of the accused to cross-examination of witnesses against him into a meaningless feature. Matters that are related to the heart of the matter as described in the indictment should not be excluded from cross-examination, and that's another issue for your Trial Chamber to consider. Finally this: The consideration of the Prosecution as set out in the paragraph 18 of their brief, namely, that a short but inadequate trial would deny both the Prosecution and the international community the right to a fair trial seems not to be valid to the amici. I already dealt with the relation between the Prosecution and the fair right -- fair trial rights guaranteed to the accused. It's obvious that non-parties in the proceedings, like the international community, do not have a right to a fair trial as guaranteed under the Statute. Let me conclude with this: The timetable is an important matter under the consideration of the Trial Chamber, but a timetable should not override the ins and outs of the fairness of a trial. These are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. One solution, Mr. Wladimiroff, may be this: to admit the statements under the Rule because they don't relate to the acts and conduct of the accused, but to require the witnesses to appear for cross-examination, in that way ensuring that where there are important issues, the accused has the ability to test the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That seems a very fair way to get out of the problem indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, the issue which we're addressing is this, as you know, whether -- there are at the moment 23, I think, witness statements which we have seen. Some more have been since served. We're not concerned with those at the moment. We are concerned with the 23 witness statements. They all relate to the evidence which is being given or to events in the evidence which is being given, and the Prosecution are asking us to admit those statements as evidence without cross-examination. The Rule provides that they can be admitted but that the -- that one of the matters which has to be considered is whether there are other factors which make it appropriate for a witness to attend for cross-examination, and we have to consider whether, when the issues are contested about which the witnesses give evidence, it's right that the witnesses should appear for cross-examination. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will, within the ten-minute time limit that you have given me, present my views too. First of all, there are no undisputed facts which the opposite side wishes to point to, because the whole indictment is questionable, or rather, false. So I do not accept anybody's testimony unless the witness appears here, although we cannot speak of the equality of arms of the two sides here at all, because a few days ago you yourself explained to me that you refused to enable me to be set free, and I think that that decision by the Trial Chamber is against the law and I think that your friends are duty-bound to complain in that regard. With respect to Prosecution witnesses, I should like to remind you that the international covenant on political, human, and other rights, Article 14, guarantees the right to cross-examination of the witness, and that exists in the American Convention, the European Convention, the African Convention, and it is also guaranteed by your own Rules and Regulations of this illegal Tribunal. So it is public interest which demands that witnesses appear. Written statements are completely unreliable, especially because of their sources, the sources from which the written statements come, because all these written statements come from environments in which all the witnesses are in the hands of the same killers who disseminated bloodshed for several years in Kosovo and Metohija. Secondly, I wish to draw your attention to the following, and that is that the five conventions guarantee a right to a public trial. Therefore, you cannot have a public character of a trial unless you enable witnesses to appear here in Court and to be subjected to cross-examination. You have the Universal Declaration, Article 10 of that declaration, Article 14 of the International Pact, then you have Article 6 of the European Convention and Article 8.5 of the American Convention, Article 5 of the American Declaration, and so on and so forth. So exceptions from public debate is only when it comes to law and order in the courtroom and public morals and law and order. Therefore, I insist upon the fact that we clarify this point fully, and we cannot accept anybody's written statement. And what we have just heard from the witnesses that have gone by so far, we see how much contradiction, how much false facts they operate with, how much mounted and rigged explanations they have, what a lot of manipulation there is between them and this false indictment. Therefore, if there is anything that must not be allowed, at any cost, is that some invisible witnesses appear here on the basis of whose statements - and we don't know who wrote the statements or what stands behind those statements - be allowed to go forward and to try a case on that basis. I am being accused here of the most horrific crimes that anybody can be accused of, and now what they want to do is to do this on the basis of some sort of secret witnesses and written statements. I think that this is - how shall I put it? - an absurdity. This is an absurd demand which cannot be accepted in any way, especially not with the explanation given here that they take up too much time. Because if one would follow that logic, and according to this false indictment, the only thing that stops all this rigged-up trial here is my presence here and the examination of witnesses and what I'm saying here. So that when we're talking about cross-examination, I have the right to cross-examine the witnesses, to test their credibility, to test the circumstances of the evidence in chief, and a series of other matters. Let us go back to the first question, and that is to stop me exercising my right, the right that you yourselves have prescribed through your Rules and Regulations. So this is not a concession on your part; it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is a right that has been written down, the right of a person to be able to defend himself. I don't want to enter into the illegality of your Tribunal here, but even as an illegal Tribunal in Court yourself, you have prescribed that very right yourselves; and on the other hand, you make it impossible physically for the accused standing before you to avail himself of that right, because there is no possibility whatsoever for me to communicate with the witnesses, to examine the witnesses, to talk to my associates, to consult people and amass facts and information which would topple all your rigged evidence which the witnesses are putting forward in conformity with the false indictment. Do you know that thousands of citizens contact my associates to challenge what they are hearing here? How can you imagine that under conditions of this kind, where I'm working from 7.00 in the morning until 6.00 in the afternoon, 6.00 p.m., losing so much time, sitting here -- I am flooded with material. I have just received this Patrick Ball material, who I hear from the Prosecutor is to be called tomorrow. The lady has provided me with this list just a moment ago, and it contains a hundred pages for me to read. How can you imagine that it is possible for me to exercise my right, the right that you have prescribed yourselves, the right physically -- I am being physically stopped from exercising my right, and then you claim that this is a fair trial and that there is equality of arms between the two parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you wouldn't have been in this position if you had read the material before. I don't know when Patrick Ball's report was disclosed to you, but I have no doubt it was some time ago. So if you had read it before, you wouldn't be in this position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That again is not true. You, as an institution here, dealing with what you deal with, you have trials that go on for several years for a concrete event linked, for example, to one locality - who knows where - whereas you here are presenting a false indictment which charges me, accuses me and my state and my nation for three wars in thousands of localities, presenting tragic events from that war individually, so as to mask an answer to the main question: Why war, why terrorism, why the crime against Yugoslavia, and why the NATO aggression? And then what you're doing now, in the thousands of different localities, over three wars, you are shortening in comparison to the other cases that you're dealing with here and trying here. And then you want to show that all this is just. Why didn't you get through all those other cases in one day? But you've been keeping people here for years. Why don't you let all those Serbs and Croats and Muslims, why don't you set them free, if you have proclaimed from the other side of the well that it is I who am responsible? Why don't you let all these other people go home, then, because you now have been given the opportunity of proving everything you wish to prove here with me here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to be clear as to your position on these statements. There are two possibilities: Firstly, the statements will not be admitted at all; secondly, the statements may be admitted but with the right to cross-examine. You have stressed your right to cross-examine, and it is in that regard that I'm seeking the clarification. If the statements were to be admitted but you would have the right to cross-examine, would you have a problem with that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There can be no compromise. A witness who has something to say must come here and say it, testify here in Court, and then be subjected to cross-examination, and not to have somebody write a statement for him and then I am going to examine a phantom statement here in Court of some individual who is prepared and who has rigged all this and serves the function of this false indictment. So my stand is categorically clear: Until the witness comes here into the Court and fulfills the right and guarantee to a complete cross-examination, we are not able to accept his testimony as any evidence or proof, and that is the case in every normal court. Of course, I don't know what it is like for your particular Court. But I think that my position there is quite clear and quite categorical. Witnesses who appear in Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice, one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Four minutes, I think. Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to draw your attention to one point, and it is an important one. What Slobodan Milosevic said a moment ago with respect to Patrick Ball, that he received the document only today, it was not until today that this document was served. It was not translated into Serbian until today. The document was not translated into Serbian, nor did the Trial Chamber make a decision in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was produced, I have no doubt, in English, so at least two of the amici would have been able to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it should have been translated, and we did not receive a translated copy, and I think the decision was made that disclosure should follow these lines. You were not asked -- all vital documents should be disclosed and submitted in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The languages of the Tribunal. Yes, Mr. Nice. Can you help us about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. The original version of Dr. Ball's report was provided months ago in English. It was resupplied last week, in answer to the accused's request following a question of mine to the Chamber, in English. It was first provided in B/C/S, in Serbian, as soon as it was available. It's a long document and it took a long time to be translated, given the other priorities that the CLSS have and that they determine, not us. It's been made available for translation at the earliest possible moment, but of course it doesn't fall for the priority that documents that have to be translated enjoy. So he's had it for months in English and last week in English as well. Can I, in a couple of minutes, make just a few other points, because I was very short in opening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you. The observations are entirely inappropriate and unacceptable of the accused about how witness statements are taken, will have to be subject to evidence and methodology, in our respectful submission, in due course. The amici's observations about the sufficiency of live evidence should nevertheless take account of the reality that if one were to call 80 live witnesses, where 800.000, it is said, have been transported or moved or whatever, then one is calling something on the basis of 1 in 10.000. We are aware and the Chamber is no doubt aware of the obvious need to have as many witnesses as possible where a sampling is of those sort of fractions. Hearsay is specifically covered in the Rules of the Tribunal and doesn't in itself exclude 92 bis. The right of cross-examination has been specifically dealt with in the provision of the ruling that allowed for 92 bis when the Chamber in Plenary Session allowed for it, and likewise taken into account were all the conventions to which the accused has referred. Therefore, they don't in themselves automatically allow him to have these witnesses before the Chamber. I very respectfully would observe that if this particular accused's mere opposition leads to a finding that then the evidence has to be in some form before this Chamber, although we personally have no objections at all, the Chamber has, of course, to have in mind the effect elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, but there's been -- it's not a question of mere opposition. There has been detailed cross-examination on the points, which have been put into issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm making the point with other cases in mind. Were the course to be adopted of the witnesses coming to be cross-examined, we would press the Chamber to say that certainly a summary of what the statements contain should be made available first, as a matter of record, or alternatively, the statements should be read out in full, if that wouldn't take too long. So, Your Honour, those, I think, are all the matters that I desire to raise by way of reply. And certainly we invite you to consider not just the two alternatives that His Honour Judge Robinson referred to but the three alternatives that remain for consideration, because it's our duty, in the interests the brevity of the case, to do that. Our position remains as it always has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We'll consider these matters and give our ruling in due course. We'll adjourn now until half past 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of March, 2002, at 9.30 a.m.
